newsitem.title: EAST TIMOR: Timorese urged not to protest at statue ceremony.
newsitem.headline: Timorese urged not to protest at statue ceremony.

text.p: Church leaders in East Timor called on residents on Sunday to refrain from protests against Indonesia's annexation of the troubled territory during a ceremony to bless a giant statue of Jesus Christ.

"I trust the people who attend will be good Catholics," said Father Jose Antonio during a short oration at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception in Dili's Vila Verde district before Nobel peace laureate Bishop Carlos Belo celebrated Mass.

One of the 2,000 parishioners at the service said the comments were in response to rumours that youths were planning to use the ceremony scheduled for later in the day to show their opposition to Jakarta's rule over the former Portuguese colony.
"I think he meant they want no interference and want things to go well," the parishioner said.

Some 25,000 people are expected to attend the blessing ceremony of the 27-metre (90-foot) high bronze statue of Christ, located about seven km east of the East Timor capital Dili and said to be the world's tallest outside Rio de Janeiro in Brazil.
Jakarta-based foreign journalists have been given permission to cover the event, one of the rare occasions when Indonesian authorities have relaxed the restricted access to East Timor.
Mainly Moslem Indonesia invaded predominantly Roman Catholic East Timor in 1975 and annexed it the following year in a move never recognised by the United Nations.
Sporadic resistance to Jakarta's rule still erupts in the territory and some 200 guerrillas are believed to be still holed up in the rugged hills in the interior.
Indonesia maintains a disproportionate military presence in East Timor compared with its neighbouring provinces, saying that the troops are needed to help development of the territory.
The troubles in East Timor have grabbed world attention since Belo and self-exiled resistance leader Jose Ramos-Horta were jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize last month.
Belo, perhaps the most-respected person in the territory, has indicated he wants no trouble during the ceremony, in which he will lead other priests in blessing the statue.
On Sunday, his sermon in the local Tetum language, with some Indonesian and Portuguese, urged parishioners to be more involved in church work. He did not refer to the ceremony.
Some residents said Belo's wishes would be respected.
"There might be some banners (at the ceremony) but they will probably say 'Viva Belo'. They are likely to be more pro-Belo than political," one youth said on Saturday.
The statue itself has raised much ire in East Timor.

Located on the top of a headland on the eastern side of Dili Bay, it was built by the Jakarta government and paid for by the national flag carrier Garuda Indonesia and is seen as a symbol of Indonesia's rule.
It is also resented by some as lowly-paid local civil servants made compulsory contributions to the statue, conceived as a tourist attraction rather than a religious monument.
Military officials said the city was calm at the weekend as trucks carrying people from outlying areas began to arrive in Dili.
